content.text: A CLAUDE.md line, however loudly it's written, is an instruction Claude reads and weighs. Claude follows it nearly every time, but on any given turn that's still Claude's call. When a rule can't have exceptions, move it into a hook or a deny rule: Claude Code applies those itself, before the action, every time. Keep that enforced set small and leave guidelines to Claude.
A payments team's CLAUDE.md says "Never edit an existing migration; add a new one." Deep in a long session about a refund bug, Claude fixes a column type by editing

, which staging applied last week. The tests rebuild their database from scratch, so they pass. Staging never re-runs 0042, and its schema quietly drifts from what the code expects. The fix someone pushes is "IMPORTANT: NEVER EDIT AN EXISTING MIGRATION!!!". The next week Claude asks before creating any file in
, even the new migration the task needs.
"A rule in CLAUDE.md is a rule, and if Claude broke it, it wasn't written strongly enough." Smart teams believe this for good reasons:

items.text: Claude does follow CLAUDE.md nearly every time, so the rare miss looks like a wording problem.
Emphasis used to help. Older models sometimes needed IMPORTANT and capital letters to notice a line.
is the documented home for project instructions and loads into every session, so it feels like configuration.
Adding a word takes five seconds. Writing a script takes an afternoon, or so it seems.

content.text: The half-truth is the first point. Claude really does follow the line almost always, and for most rules almost is exactly right. But as Anthropic's best-practices guide puts it, no matter how strongly you word a line, "whether Claude follows that line on a given turn is still Claude's call."

The docs sort everything you give Claude Code into two kinds. Non-deterministic instructions are read by the model, which then decides what to do with them: your prompt, CLAUDE.md, a skill. Deterministic ones are configured, and Claude Code, the harness around the model, "has to execute" them: hooks, deny rules, managed settings. The memory guide is just as direct: Claude treats CLAUDE.md "as context, not enforced configuration", and to block an action "regardless of what Claude decides", you use a
Emphasis changes the weighting, not the guarantee

Capital letters don't move a line from the first kind to the second. They make Claude weigh it more heavily, and the docs warn that piling on emphasis "mostly makes Claude over-apply the rule": the team above traded a missed rule for a nervous one. The guide's own test: if you keep adding emphasis and Claude still misses the line, "that's a sign the line belongs in a hook."
A hook runs before the action
is your command, attached to a point in Claude's loop. A
hook fires after Claude has prepared a tool call and before Claude Code runs it. Claude Code pipes the call to your script as JSON on stdin:

items.text: : no objection. The call goes through the normal permission flow; exit 0 doesn't approve it.
: the call is blocked, and whatever you wrote to stderr reaches Claude as the tool's error, so it can change course instead of retrying blindly.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Database
- IMPORTANT: NEVER EDIT AN EXISTING MIGRATION!!!
- ALWAYS add a new one instead. NO EXCEPTIONS.

content.text: The script holds the logic. "Existing" here means committed: a migration you've committed may already run somewhere, while a new file Claude is still writing stays editable.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse hook: committed migrations are immutable
set -e  # a missing jq exits non-zero instead of allowing the edit
FILE_PATH=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty')
FILE_PATH="${FILE_PATH//\\//}"  # normalize Windows separators

if [[ "$FILE_PATH" == */db/migrations/* ]] &&
  git -C "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" ls-files --error-unmatch \
    "$FILE_PATH" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Blocked: $FILE_PATH is committed and may be applied." >&2
  echo "Add a new migration: pnpm db:migrate:new <name>" >&2
  exit 2
fi

exit 0  # no decision: the normal permission flow applies

How to apply it in your project
Search your CLAUDE.md files for IMPORTANT, NEVER, ALWAYS and capital letters. Each one is a rule someone found hard to get followed.
If the rule has exceptions, rewrite it plainly and leave it to Claude. If it has none, it needs enforcement.
